SEC12A-01.note: Participial phrase must open the second clause to modify 'dome'; B comma splice, C attaches the participle to the seismometers clause (misplaced) and is the strongest distractor, D run-on is free. PHASE 2: Key and explanation agree; C's misplaced-modifier rationale is stated correctly.

SEC12A-02.note: Opening dash after 'butterfly' must be closed by a dash before 'remains'. Resolving signal is BEFORE the blank (the opening dash). Semicolon between subject and verb is a free strike. PHASE 2: Correct. Ship.

SEC12A-03.note: Relative clause opened by a comma after 'scribe' must close with a comma; the interior dash pair is a good lure toward B. D makes 'also illustrated' a second relative-clause verb and leaves no main verb. A is a free strike. PHASE 2: Correct; good dash-pair lure. Same template as B-06 in this batch.

SEC12A-04.note: Colon introduces a semicolon-separated list after a complete clause. A yields a fragment (free strike); B semicolon before a non-clause; C comma cannot introduce a list whose items are separated by semicolons. PHASE 2: Correct. Ship.

SEC12A-05.note: 'However' is an interrupter inside one clause after a long introductory prepositional phrase; B's semicolon leaves a fragment and is the reflex answer. C (no comma before however) free strike; D needs the closing comma. PHASE 2: Correct; the reflexive semicolon-however lure is the item's strength.

SEC12A-06.note: Noun clause 'whether ... oxide of the metal' is the SUBJECT of 'remained', so a full boundary is needed. A invites reading 'whether' as an adverbial clause and is a strong lure; the resolving verb 'remained' is ~15 words after the blank. D 'as to whether' is malformed with 'remained'. PHASE 2: Correct; best item in the batch.

SEC12A-07.note: 'Remarkably little loss of strength...' has no verb, so B and D produce obvious fragments; A leaves a dangling noun phrase. C is the only option that changes a word (adds 'with'), an odd-one-out tell; SEC boundary items normally keep the words fixed. Borderline blueprint. PHASE 2: Key correct, but the key is the only option that adds a word, and B/D are visible fragments. That is a free odd-one-out pick, off the usual SEC boundary-item shape. Drop or re-author with fixed words.

SEC12B-01.note: Postponed direct object: 'makes visible to anyone with ... microscope the ... filaments'. No punctuation may separate verb and object; A's comma is a strong lure because the long phrase invites a pause. C fragment is a free strike. PHASE 2: Correct; strong postponed-object item.

SEC12B-02.note: Comma + 'but' joins two independent clauses; 'because' clause is introductory to the second. A (comma after 'but', none before) is the strongest distractor; it is wrong under SAT convention and under CMOS for clauses this long, but a lenient reading of the optional comma before a short-clause conjunction is the only route to a second answer. PHASE 2: Correct; explanation handles the 'but,' lure properly.

SEC12B-03.note: Colon after complete clause introducing the explanation of 'something'. C run-on and D ungrammatical 'which the mapmaker had first sketched the shoreline' strike on sight; only A (comma splice) needs a check. PHASE 2: Correct but easy; do not label it hard.

SEC12B-04.note: Summative appositive 'a pattern that suggests...' after a dash. B and C leave the same visible fragment; D no punctuation. Once one sees 'a pattern that' is not a clause, B and C fall together. PHASE 2: Correct but easy (B and C fall together); not hard-route.

SEC12B-05.note: Textbook semicolon + however between two independent clauses. B and C free strikes; A comma splice is the only distractor requiring thought. Well-practised pattern; not hard-route material. PHASE 2: Correct but textbook semicolon-however; easy for the hard route. Fine as a medium filler, not as hard.

SEC12B-06.note: Close the comma-opened 'which...and which' clause before main verb 'shares'. Same template as A-03 (comma-opened relative clause with an interior interrupter, close with comma). Semicolon between subject and verb is a free strike. PHASE 2: Correct; structurally a twin of A-03, so do not seat both on one form.

SEC12B-07.note: 'Only after ... did mills begin' is inverted main-clause syntax, so it must start a sentence; A is a comma splice. The resolving 'did' is far after the blank. D 'although only after ... did' is malformed (free strike). PHASE 2: Correct. Ship.
